'''''Silene nutans''''' is a [[flowering plant]] in the genus ''[[Silene]]'', most commonly known as '''Nottingham catchfly'''.<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref>

==Description==
''Silene nutans'' is a diploid, mainly [[outcrossing]], [[herb]]aceous, [[perennial plant]].<ref name="Rossum"/>
It grows up to {{convert|25|-|80|cm|0}} tall, from a branching, [[wood]]y stock with a thick [[taproot]].<ref name="EFBI">{{cite web |website=Ecological Flora of the British Isles |title=''Silene nutans'' |access-date=January 12, 2010 |url=http://www.ecoflora.co.uk/search_species2.php?plant_no=570280150}}</ref> The lower leaves are up to {{convert|75|mm|0}} long, [[:wikt:spathulate|spathulate]] and have a long stalk, while leaves higher on the plant are [[:wikt:lanceolate|lanceolate]], [[:wikt:subsessile|subsessile]] and acute; all the leaves are covered in soft hairs.<ref name="EFBI"/> The flowers are {{convert|18|mm|1}} wide, {{convert|12|mm|1}} long, and drooping, on short, [[:wikt:viscid|viscid]] stalks. The petals are white or pinkish and divided into two narrow lobes. Each flower remains open for three nights as a means of preventing [[self-fertilisation]]; the flower reveals one [[Whorl (botany)|whorl]] of [[stamen]]s on the first night, the second whorl of stamens on the second night, and the three [[style (botany)|styles]] on the third night.<ref name="EFBI"/> The seeds are {{convert|10|-|22|mm|1}} wide and [[kidney]]-shaped.<ref name="EFBI"/>

==Distribution==
''Silene nutans'' is widespread across Europe, from southern Spain and Italy north to the British Isles and Scandinavia, and is also found across large parts of Asia.<ref name="AFE"/> It has been introduced to North America, where it is known as the '''Eurasian catchfly'''. It is found in the U.S. states of [[Michigan]], [[Ohio]], [[New York (state)|New York]], [[Vermont]] and [[Maine]].<ref>{{PLANTS | taxon = Silene nutans'' L. (Eurasian catchfly)'' | symbol = SINU2 | accessdate = January 12, 2010}}</ref>

''Silene nutans'' can sometimes be found in the very widespread [[British NVC community MG1|MG1 (''Arrhenatherum elatius'' grassland)]] community of the [[British National Vegetation Classification]], and thus can be found where ''[[Arrhenatherum elatius]]'' (false oat grass) or ''[[Dactylis glomerata]]'' (cocksfoot) occur.<ref>{{cite book |author=John S. Rodwell |year=1992 |series=[[British Plant Communities (series of books)|British Plant Communities]] |title=Volume 3 - Grasslands and montane communities |isbn=978-0-521-39166-5|author-link=John S. Rodwell }}</ref>

==Ecology==
''Silene nutans'' is a [[steppe]] species across most of its range. At the periphery of its [[Species distribution|distribution]], it has a patchy distribution in [[xeric]] habitats, such as open [[grassland]]s and on rock [[outcrop]]s at forest margins, on both acidic and alkaline substrates ([[pH]] 3.8–8.0).<ref name="Rossum">{{cite journal |journal=[[Heredity (journal)|Heredity]] |year=1997 |volume=78 |pages=552–560 |doi=10.1038/hdy.1997.86 |title=Allozyme variation in relation to ecotypic differentiation and population size in marginal populations of ''Silene nutans'' |author=Fabienne van Rossum, Xavier Vekemans, Pierre Meerts, Emmanuelle Gratia & Claude Lefèbvre |issue=5|doi-access=free }}</ref> In the far north of its range, ''S. nutans'' is characteristic of maritime [[cliff]]s.<ref>{{cite book |chapter-url=http://www.angus.gov.uk/biodiversity/pdf/Section%202/Coast%20and%20Estuaries/CE2.pdf |publisher=[[Angus Council]] |access-date=January 12, 2010 |chapter=Maritime Cliff and Slope CE2 |editor=Catherine A. G. Lloyd |title=Tayside Local Biodiversity Action Plan}}</ref>

''Silene nutans'' flowers during the night, and produces a strong [[floral scent]] to attract its [[pollinator]]s, which are mostly night-flying moths. [[Chemical compound]]s in the scent include [[benzyl acetate]] and [[benzaldehyde]].<ref>{{cite journal |journal=[[Biochemical Systematics and Ecology]] |volume=30 |issue=5 |year=2002 |pages=383–397 |doi=10.1016/S0305-1978(01)00106-5 |title=Flower scent composition in night-flowering ''Silene'' species (Caryophyllaceae) |author1=A. Jürgens, T. Witt  |author2=G. Gottsberger |name-list-style=amp }}</ref>

''Silene nutans'' is the [[host plant]] for the [[leaf miner|leaf mining]] moth ''[[Coleophora galbulipennella]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.leafmines.co.uk/html/Lepidoptera/C.galbulipennella.htm |website=British Leafminers |title=551 ''Coleophora galbulipennella'' (Zeller,1858) |access-date=January 12, 2010}}</ref>

==Nottingham==
The [[common name]] Nottingham catchfly commemorates the former occurrence of ''S. nutans'' on the walls of [[Nottingham Castle]],<ref>{{cite book |chapter-url=http://www.nottshistory.org.uk/swinnerton1910/chapter8.htm |chapter=8. Natural History |title=Nottinghamshire |series=Cambridge County Geographies |author=Henry Hurd Swinnerton |year=1910|author-link=Henry Hurd Swinnerton }}</ref> and the species was chosen to represent the [[unitary authority]] of [[Nottingham]] as its [[County flowers of the United Kingdom|county flower]].<ref>Plantlife website [http://www.plantlife.org.uk/wild_plants/county_flowers/ ''County Flowers page''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150430170312/http://www.plantlife.org.uk/wild_plants/county_flowers/ |date=2015-04-30 }}</ref> Despite this association, Nottingham catchflies no longer occur in either the city of Nottingham<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/1461011/The-floral-emblem-of-your-county.html |work=[[Daily Telegraph]] |date=May 5, 2004 |title=The floral emblem of your county}}</ref> or the wider county of [[Nottinghamshire]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nottinghamshire.gov.uk/home/environment/countryside/nature_conservation/biodiversity.htm |title=Biodiversity |publisher=[[Nottinghamshire County Council]] |access-date=January 12, 2010}}</ref>

Nottingham Castle Trust asked volunteers to grow the plant from seeds supplied to donate the successful plants back to the City to commemorate the re-opening of the renovation of Nottingham Castle.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nottinghamcastle.org.uk/nottingham-catchfly-the-project-so-far/|title=Nottingham Catchfly: The Project So Far|date=3 March 2021}}</ref>
